60_marg11: Bede. On the Acts of the Apostles he says that Paul came to the faith in the year of the passion and resurrection of Christ; and that in the thirteenth year after Christ’s passion he received the apostleship of the Gentiles, with Barnabas, and the name of Paul. For before he was called Saul, after Saul the persecutor, because as that one persecuted David, so this one persecuted the Church. In the fourteenth year, according to the agreement of the apostles, he set out for the teaching of the Gentiles.
60_marg12: He chose this name for himself for no other reason than to show himself small, as the least of the apostles. Not from any boasting, but from Saul he was made Paul, that is, from proud, little. For Paul is interpreted “little” and “quiet”; Saul, “restlessness” and “temptation.”
60_marg13: Moreover, he is said to have done this according to the custom of the holy apostles, who, advancing in virtues, were called by a changed name, so that they might be new even in the name itself, as Cephas and the sons of thunder.

60_marg15: In the Scriptures we find some with two names, some with three, as Solomon, who is also Ecclesiastes and Idida, and Matthew, who is also Levi. 60_marg16: Paul means wonderful or chosen. The Lord himself called him “a vessel of election,” and made him wonderful both in life and in teaching.

60_marg22: Christ. Although it is not a proper name but a name of sacrament, like prophet and priest, it is rightly set forth as known to the Jews. Though these names were given to many, still they are only figures; for here he alone is the true king and priest.

60_marg30: And though unmade according to the divine nature. So great is the union of both natures that the whole is called God, the whole man; and in turn man is called God, and God man; which is not so in the substances of man.
60_marg31: Who was made to him. Who was made according to the flesh, by the work of the Holy Spirit, of the Virgin, that is, born. This meets the impiety of the heretics, who with dull heart, understanding this passage, take Christ to be only man. For by adding “according to the flesh,” he reserved to the divinity its own dignity, in which Christ is the Word of God, by whom all things were made.
60_marg32: He was made according to the flesh, God made man, who even in assuming flesh did not cease to be God, remaining unchangeable, while the changeable man was assumed, the nature of man assumed not diminishing his nature.
60_marg33: He who was, was made; the Word was, the Son of God was; he was made the son of man. He took up humanity; he did not lose divinity. Born according to the truth of nature of God, the Son of God; and according to the truth of nature of man, the son of man; so that not by adoption or by name, but truly, in each nativity, he would have the name of son by being born.
60_marg34: The Son of God is therefore equal to God the Father in nature, less in condition; in the form of God, the Word begotten of God. In the form of a servant he was made of a woman. In the form of God he made man. In the form of a servant he was made man; in each, both God and both man.
60_marg35: The Word was made flesh, yet not converted and changed into what was made, but clothed with flesh, that he might appear suitably clothed for those of flesh.
60_marg36: Both forms are in Christ, because both substances are true and full in Christ. For the natures are united to each other without change and without alteration, neither does the divine depart from its own simplicity, nor is the human either changed into the nature of the deity or into non-existence, nor was one composite nature made out of the two.
60_marg37: Christ therefore is one person of twofold substance; yet God and man cannot be called a part of this person. Otherwise the Son of God, before he took the form of a servant, was not whole, and grew when man was added to his divinity.
60_marg38: “Not always to have been made” refers to creation, as there: “Lord, thou hast been made our refuge.” For the definition or publication of creation is not declared here, but he is said to be a refuge for us, which he was not before.
60_marg39: Who was made, etc. This word signifies something. For because the flesh of the Lord was not conceived from human seed in the Virgin’s womb and made a body, but by the working and power of the Holy Spirit, therefore the Apostle says made, not born.
60_marg40: Although the seed of man did not intervene in the conception of the Virgin, yet because Christ was formed from that flesh which comes from seed, he is rightly said to be made of the seed. Yet he is not therefore a creature. Whence: “All things were made by him.” It says “all things” only of what were made, that is, every creature; whence it plainly appears that he is not made, by whom all things were made.
60_marg41: For he is the true and proper Son by origin, not by adoption; in truth, not in name; by birth, not by creation.

60_marg42: Of the seed of David. Augustine. Haimo. Because Mary was of David. The promise was made to Abraham and to David, but he preferred here to say David, who was also sinful, not Abraham the just, so that he might be thought born of him not by merit but by grace; and so that he might be shown born of a king according to the flesh, as he was born a king of God before the ages.

60_marg43: Who was predestined. Predestination is the preparation of grace, by which from eternity God prepared, without merits, good things for the man Christ and for all whom he foreknew, to be made conformable to the image of his Son.
60_marg44: Foreknowledge concerns good and evil; predestination is only of the just.
60_marg45: Predestination is not foreknowledge, which pertains equally to good and bad. But it is the ordering and preparation of helping those whom divine providence finds worthy; it is properly said only of the good.
60_marg46: Who was predestinated: he who lay hidden in the flesh as to what he was, was predestinated, that is, foreknown from eternity to be manifested the Son of God in the power of rising again; but when they rise. And he says not “by the resurrection of Christ” but “of the dead,” which is a greater power, because his resurrection makes the general resurrection. Whence he seems to have destroyed death in order to redeem us; wherefore he also calls him our Lord, who gave both such grace and the power of the apostleship in his stead.
60_marg47: This so great and so lofty a union of the human nature was predestinated, so that it would have nowhere higher to be raised; just as for us the divinity itself had nowhere lower to abase itself than by taking up the nature of man with the infirmity of flesh even to the death of the cross.
60_marg48: The Apostle here speaks not of the Word but of the man, who did not exist before he was made. For that humanity, which was not before, was predestined.
60_marg49: For the most brilliant light of predestination and grace is the mediator of God and men himself, “the man Christ Jesus.” For that man, that he might be assumed by the Word, co-eternal with the Father, into the unity of person and be the only-begotten Son of God, whence did he merit this? What good of his, of whatever kind, went before, that he should come to this ineffable excellence? It was by the Word of God making and receiving him. The man himself, from the moment he began to be, began to be the only Son of God. That woman full of grace conceived of the Holy Spirit; of the Virgin Mary the only God was born, not by the desire of the flesh, but by the sole gift of God. In that man the will was free, and the more so the less he was able to sin.
60_marg50: Rightly indeed is the Son of God said to be predestinated, not according to that which he is, the Word of God, God with God. For why should he be predestinated, when he already was, who was already everlasting, without beginning and without end? But that was to be predestinated which was not yet, that so in its own time it should come to be, as before times it had been predestinated that it should come to be. Whoever therefore denies that the Son of God was predestinated, denies that same one to be the Son of man. Jesus therefore was predestinated, that he who was to be according to the flesh the son of David, should be in power the Son of God.
60_marg51: Ambrose. Whatever the Word of the Father has by nature, the son of the Virgin has by grace.

60_marg82: For the justice of God. Haimo. Ambrose. This is against the Jews, who deny that this is the Christ whom God promised.
60_marg83: Is revealed. Augustine. He attacks the Gentiles according to their former state, because they boasted of a good nature and excused their shameful deeds by ignorance. But the Apostle says on the contrary that they had earlier had knowledge, and lost it by fault, and that the good nature left to themselves was cast headlong into all evils. Having commended the piety of faith, by which, being justified, we ought to be pleasing to God, he adds, detesting the contrary, that puffed up by themselves they fell into idols.

60_marg84: From faith: of God promising, unto the faith of man who believes him. Or from faith unto faith, on account of all the parts of faith: from the faith of the Old Testament, where there is one God, unto the faith of the New, where there are the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. From the faith of the first coming unto the faith of the second. From the faith of the first resurrection unto the faith of the second. From the faith of promise unto the faith of fulfilment. From the faith of the preachers unto the faith of the peoples. From the faith of the sowers unto the faith of the reapers. He has justice who passes from faith to faith, so that the Jew and anyone else may pass from the faith of the Old Testament to the faith of the New, and from the faith of words and hope to the faith of realities and of sight.
60_marg85: “Faith is that by which are believed those things which are not seen.” There is also faith when one believes, not by words but by present realities, what will be when God shall give himself to be seen. He says therefore from the faith of words, by which we believe what we do not see, unto the faith of realities, by which we shall obtain what we believed.

For from the very fabric of heaven God is shown angry with them, who made the stars so beautiful that from them it might be known how great and how wonderful their creator is, and so he alone be adored.

And therefore he is to be believed to work well or ill, and deservedly to be saved or condemned. I say to work well and to be saved, which is not possible except through grace and faith, which renews the natural image of God in man, lulled asleep by vice and age; without this renewal he works ill and is condemned, his conscience accusing him; for vice is against nature, and this grace heals. For in that Trinity is the highest origin of all things, and the most perfect beauty, and the most blessed love. And so those three seem to be distinguished from one another, and are also infinite in themselves, so that each is in each, and all in each, and each in all, and all are one. What the Apostle says is therefore not to be taken confusedly: Of him, and by him, and in him. Of him, he says on account of the Father; by him, on account of the Son; in him, on account of the Holy Ghost. Reasonably it can be seen of evil power as well, since the good are purified by it and the wicked are condemned and it itself is cast down into the worse. The malice of men has of itself the desire to harm, but power, if God does not give it, it does not have; and therefore the devil, before he took anything from Job, said to the Lord: “Put forth thy hand,” that is, give power. 60_marg742: God alone is properly called “eternal,” because he is without beginning and without end. Not so eternal fire, which, though without end, yet has a beginning. That, then, is true eternity which is true immortality; this is that highest unchangeableness which God alone has, that he cannot be changed at all. For it is one thing for something not to be changed though it can be changed, another not to be able to be changed at all. So, then, man is called good, yet not as God, of whom it is said: “None is good but God alone.” So the soul of man is called immortal, yet not as God, of whom it is said: “Who only hath immortality.” So also man is called wise, yet not as God, of whom it is said: “To God the only wise.” So fire is called eternal, yet not as God, whose immortality alone is itself true eternity.

60_marg743: This error has crept in upon some, who suppose that the Father alone is signified here, and that he alone is truly wise; whereas it is not said, “to the only wise Father,” but “to God the only wise,” and the one God is the Trinity itself, so that we understand God alone to be wise as we understand God alone to be powerful, that is, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, who is the one and only God whom alone we are commanded to serve. Yet if the Apostle had said, “to the only wise Father,” he would not thereby separate the Son or the Holy Spirit. As in the Apocalypse it is read of the Son, who “hath a name written which no man knoweth, but he that receiveth it”; yet the Father, from whom the Son is inseparable, is not therefore said not to know this name. As, then, the Father knows what no one is said to know but the Son, because the Father and the Son are inseparable, so also, had it been said “to the only wise Father,” the Son and the Holy Spirit would have to be understood together with him, because they are inseparable.
